archive.title: New DNA sequencing methods detect rare mutations acquired as bodies grow and age
archive.summary: Somatic mutations, the DNA changes that occur as our bodies grow and age, not only hold an important key to cancer but are emerging as the seeds of a wide range of common, noncancerous diseases. The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network, a National Institutes of Health Common Fund initiative to catalog all the normal processes of somatic mutation, has published its first comprehensive benchmarking study in the journal Cell. The researchers developed and calibrated new sequencing technologies, experimental approaches and computational methods that now make it possible to detect different types of somatic mutations with greater sensitivity and specificity than ever before.

archive.title: Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
archive.summary: Researchers led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University have discovered a protein that may allow harmful aging cells to escape detection by the immune system. By helping these cells remain in the body instead of being cleared away, the protein could contribute to their accumulation and the development of health problems associated with aging. The discovery, published in Cell Metabolism, identifies PD-L2 as a potential target for therapies aimed at eliminating harmful aging cells. Scientists also believe the protein could serve as a blood marker, providing a way to detect and monitor these cells.
archive.displayTitle: Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
archive.originalSummary: Scientists have discovered a protein that may help harmful aging cells hide from the immune system, allowing them to accumulate and fuel age-related health problems. Blocking the protein in mice reduced these cells and inflammation while improving blood sugar regulation and strength, offering a promising new direction for anti-aging research.

archive.title: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses
archive.summary: The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from Donald Trump. Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to. Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it is the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.

archive.title: Albania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protests
archive.summary: Albania’s prime minister has said he will not resign as a protest movement, initially prompted by a proposal to build a Trump family-backed resort in the Balkan state, turned violent with clashes convulsing the capital for a third consecutive day. Speaking on Thursday after calls by students who this week assumed control of the anti-government demonstrations that have rattled Tirana since June, Edi Rama said: “Governments are changed through democratic elections. We had elections last year, not a revolution.” Rama’s comments to Reuters came hours before fresh clashes erupted outside the education ministry, where riot police responded to rock-throwing youths with teargas and water cannon.

archive.title: Ancient Hole in Neanderthal Shoulder Blade May Be The Oldest Spear Attack Ever Discovered
archive.summary: The left scapula of Shanidar A. (University of Cambridge) When the end came, it must have been very painful. In a moment of violence roughly 75,000 years ago, something sharp pierced the body of the victim, known only as Shanidar A, an adult Neanderthal estimated to be 45 years old. The deadly injury left a gaping 15-millimeter-wide hole in Shanidar A's left shoulder blade. We can't say for sure what made that hole, but in a new study in Scientific Reports, researchers suggest it was probably a spear, meaning this could be the earliest known example of an interpersonal spear attack in the hominin fossil record.

archive.title: America's historic preservation law is in peril, advocates say. Here's what's at stake
archive.summary: It's been exactly 60 years since President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) into law, alongside half a dozen conservation bills. "We have come here this morning to give part of our country back to its people," Johnson declared at the bill signing on Oct. 15, 1966. Now, historic preservation advocates say, the government is trying to yank the public's power away. "Preservation, from its inception, has worked best with public and private partnership," Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation, told NPR. "Over the last year and a half, the federal government has divested that responsibility."

archive.originalSummary: Congress and a federal agency are threatening to weaken the country's historic preservation law, fueling a backlash that critics say is as fiery as the one that led to the law's creation 60 years ago.

archive.title: Satellite data reveal how Antarctica’s ice cliffs behave over time
archive.summary: With rising temperatures, the buttressing ice shelves at the edges the Antarctic ice sheet are melting and calving off at record rates, leaving behind sheer cliffs of solid ice. The stability of these exposed ice cliffs could influence how Antarctica further breaks apart and contributes to sea level rise around the world. Scientists have assumed that an ice cliff’s stability depends on its height: Ice cliffs that are taller than 100 meters — about the height of the Statue of Liberty — should collapse under their own weight. And once a cliff sloughs off, it should expose even taller, inland cliffs that collapse in turn.
archive.displayTitle: Satellite data reveal how Antarctica’s ice cliffs behave over time
archive.originalSummary: The cliffs don’t always collapse in the runaway process that scientists had expected.

archive.title: Laser pulses bring order to a quantum material's tiny electrical regions
archive.summary: Physicists at Auburn University have used flashes of laser light to bring order to tiny electrically charged "islands" inside a crystal. The discovery helps answer a decades-old question about how the material organizes itself and shows how light could be used to control its behavior—a step toward exploring new technologies for processing and storing information. The research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter endowed associate professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil. Their study, "Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition," was selected as an Editors' Suggestion in Physical Review Letters.

archive.title: Quantum calculations reveal how spin defects lose energy
archive.summary: When light hits a tiny defect embedded in a solid material like diamond or silicon carbide, it can kick the defect's electrons into an excited state. These spin defects have the potential to be used as stable, readable qubits for quantum technologies, for example, quantum sensing. But modeling the full physics of their energetics over time—a key step in developing spin defects into new technologies—is a challenging task. Now, researchers at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME) have built a computational framework that captures the full optical cycle of such spin defects, including the prediction of internal conversion, a process particularly hard to model.

archive.title: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
archive.summary: Scientists have uncovered a promising new way to protect some of the world's most important food crops from a destructive fungus that threatens global food security. By engineering the natural immune defenses of plants, researchers have developed an experimental approach that could eventually help wheat, rice, and barley resist fungal infections more effectively. The international research team, led by scientists at the John Innes Centre in the United Kingdom, investigated a recently discovered group of plant immune receptors. They identified how these proteins recognize invading pathogens and demonstrated that they can be modified to detect multiple fungal threats.
archive.displayTitle: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
archive.originalSummary: Scientists have discovered a potential new weapon against a devastating fungus that threatens rice, wheat, and barley worldwide. By engineering a special type of plant immune receptor, researchers created defenses capable of recognizing multiple fungal threats at once. The breakthrough could eventually lead to crops with powerful, long-lasting disease resistance, helping protect a global food supply increasingly threatened by spreading infections and climate change.

archive.title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
archive.summary: Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured. The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden". A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.

archive.title: Healthy Coral Reversed Bleaching in Its Neighbor With Just 1 Week of Contact
archive.summary: Corals cannot survive long without the algae that live inside their bodies. But under stress from factors like heat, pollution, and UV exposure, these algae can become toxic to the coral, which evicts them. Without their algal symbionts, corals turn white, in what is known as coral bleaching. A 'bleached' coral has limited time to acquire new algal symbionts before it starves to death. With the threat of coral bleaching events growing each year, Stanford scientists have found a technique that could help rescue corals on the brink of death. "While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet," says Stanford marine scientist Danny Collins.
